analogy.p: Think of the carbon footprint as a till receipt that lists every greenhouse gas 'purchase' made while a product was grown, made, delivered, used and thrown away; the total at the bottom is the footprint. Reducing the footprint means removing items from the receipt (efficiency), switching to cheaper-carbon brands (alternative energy) or paying a charge on each item (carbon tax). The analogy breaks down because a receipt shows one price per item, while real greenhouse gases build up in the atmosphere over time and different gases trap different amounts of heat.
analogy.t: A shopping receipt for the planet

bullets: Definition to learn word for word: the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
It applies to three kinds of thing: a **product** (a phone, a pair of trainers), a **service** (a bus route, a hospital) and an **event** (a football match, a music festival).
It is usually quoted as a mass of carbon dioxide (or 'carbon dioxide equivalent', which converts other gases such as methane into the amount of CO2 that would warm the Earth by the same amount).
A bigger footprint means more greenhouse gas released, so more energy trapped in the atmosphere and a greater contribution to global warming.
It is a **measure of impact**, not a measure of pollution in the toxic sense: carbon dioxide is not poisonous at normal levels, it is a problem because of its effect on climate.
The footprint can be calculated for a person or country too, by adding up everything they buy, burn and use in a year.
core.p: The **carbon footprint** is the total amount of **carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases** emitted over the **full life cycle** of a **product, service or event**. It is a way of putting a single measure on how much a thing, an activity or a person contributes to the enhanced greenhouse effect and so to global climate change. The word 'carbon' is shorthand: the footprint includes methane and other greenhouse gases as well as carbon dioxide, and the key phrase examiners look for is 'over the full life cycle'.

bullets: **Obtaining raw materials**: mining ores, drilling for crude oil, cutting down and processing trees, growing crops. Machinery burns fuel, and clearing land removes trees that would have absorbed carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
**Manufacturing**: factories use electricity and heat, usually from burning fossil fuels, and some chemical processes release carbon dioxide directly (for example making cement or extracting iron).
**Transport**: lorries, ships and planes burn fossil fuels, so goods that travel further have a larger footprint at this stage.
**Use**: a car burns petrol or diesel, a kettle uses electricity, a gas boiler burns methane. For many products the use stage is the biggest part.
**Disposal**: rubbish decomposing in landfill releases **methane**; incineration releases carbon dioxide; recycling needs energy but usually less than making from new.
Packaging, storage and shop lighting also add to the footprint.
The sum of the emissions at every stage is the carbon footprint, which links directly to a **life cycle assessment**.
core.h: The full life cycle: where the emissions come from
core.p: To work out a carbon footprint you must follow the product or service through every stage of its life, not just the stage you can see. Greenhouse gases are released when raw materials are obtained, when the product is made, when it is moved around the world, when it is used by the customer and finally when it is thrown away or recycled. Many students forget the stages before and after use, so mark schemes reward answers that name several different stages.

bullets: The **carbon footprint can be reduced by reducing emissions of carbon dioxide and methane**: this is the statement the specification makes.
Water vapour is the third greenhouse gas you must know, but human activity does not directly control it, so footprints concentrate on CO2 and CH4.
Greenhouse gases absorb **long-wavelength (infrared) radiation** emitted by the warm surface and re-radiate it in all directions, including back to Earth.
Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere, so the atmosphere does not block incoming energy as effectively as outgoing energy.
Because a methane molecule traps much more heat than a carbon dioxide molecule, reducing methane can be an efficient way to cut a footprint.
Higher tier thinking: carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere for a very long time, whereas methane breaks down more quickly, so the two behave differently over decades.
core.h: Greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide and methane
core.p: Two gases dominate the topic. **Carbon dioxide** is released whenever carbon-containing fuels burn and when living things respire. **Methane** is a much stronger greenhouse gas per molecule, but there is far less of it in the atmosphere and it does not last as long. Both absorb long-wavelength infrared radiation re-emitted from the Earth's surface and radiate some of it back, which keeps the planet warmer than it would otherwise be. Adding more of either strengthens this effect.

bullets: Burning fossil fuels: carbon in the fuel combines with oxygen, e.g. CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, releasing carbon dioxide that was locked underground for millions of years.
Deforestation: fewer trees means less carbon dioxide removed by photosynthesis, and if the wood is burned or rots it releases carbon dioxide too.
Cattle and sheep: microorganisms in their guts produce methane, which is released by the animal.
Rice paddy fields: waterlogged soil has little oxygen, so microorganisms break down organic matter and release methane.
Landfill: buried food and garden waste is decomposed by microorganisms with little oxygen, producing methane.
Natural gas leaks from pipes and wells release methane directly, since natural gas is mostly methane.
Producing cement and some metals releases carbon dioxide from the chemical reactions as well as from the fuel burned.
core.h: Main human sources of carbon dioxide and methane
core.p: You must be able to name the human activities that increase the amounts of these gases. For carbon dioxide the major source is the **combustion of fossil fuels** (coal, oil, natural gas) for electricity, heating and transport, together with **deforestation**, which removes trees that take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. For methane the major sources are **livestock** (cattle and sheep produce it in digestion), **rice paddy fields** (where bacteria decompose plant material without oxygen) and **decomposition of rubbish in landfill sites**.

bullets: Wind, solar and hydroelectric produce **no carbon dioxide when generating electricity**, so electricity from them has a small footprint per unit.
Wind and solar are **intermittent** (depend on wind and sunshine), so back-up supplies or energy storage are needed, which adds cost.
Nuclear power produces no carbon dioxide in operation but has high building costs, produces radioactive waste and carries public safety concerns.
Biofuels (such as bioethanol from sugar cane) are made from plants that absorbed carbon dioxide as they grew, so they can reduce net emissions, but growing them can use land needed for food.
Building the equipment (turbines, panels, dams) has its own footprint, which is why you must think about the whole life cycle.
Using alternative fuels in transport, for example electric vehicles charged from renewable electricity, shifts emissions away from the exhaust pipe.
core.h: Reducing the footprint: alternative energy supplies
core.p: One action is **increased use of alternative energy supplies instead of fossil fuels**. Wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal and nuclear power stations release little or no carbon dioxide while they generate electricity, so replacing coal and gas power stations lowers the footprint of everything powered by that electricity. Biofuels are another alternative. However, each option has costs and limits, so a good answer always weighs advantages against disadvantages.

bullets: Domestic examples: loft and cavity wall insulation, double glazing, LED light bulbs, efficient boilers, turning appliances off instead of leaving them on standby.
Industrial examples: recovering waste heat from furnaces to preheat materials, using heat exchangers, using more efficient motors, and running processes at lower temperatures with catalysts.
Efficiency means **a greater proportion of the input energy is transferred usefully**, so fewer units of fuel are burned for the same output.
Insulation reduces thermal energy transfer to the surroundings, so less fuel is needed to keep a building warm.
Better public transport and car sharing increase the efficiency with which people are moved, reducing fuel use per person.
The saving is real only if the money or energy saved is not spent on something that emits even more (the 'rebound effect' at higher tier thinking).
core.p: A second action is **increased energy efficiency in domestic and industrial processes**. If a process wastes less energy then less fuel needs to be burned to do the same job, so less carbon dioxide is released. Efficiency measures are often cheap and pay for themselves, which makes them popular, but they rely on people and companies investing in them and changing habits.

bullets: Step 1: **capture** the carbon dioxide from the flue gases (for example by absorbing it in a solvent).
Step 2: **compress** it to a liquid-like dense fluid and **transport** it, usually by pipeline.
Step 3: **store** it permanently underground in depleted oil and gas fields or deep saline rock formations.
Advantage: allows continued use of fossil fuel power stations and heavy industry while greatly cutting emissions.
Disadvantages: very high cost, the energy needed for capture and compression, limited suitable storage sites and the risk of **leakage** back to the atmosphere.
It does nothing about the carbon dioxide released when the fossil fuel was mined and transported unless those emissions are also controlled.
core.h: Reducing the footprint: carbon capture and storage
core.p: **Carbon capture and storage (CCS)** removes carbon dioxide from waste gases before they reach the atmosphere. The gas is separated from the exhaust of power stations or factories, compressed, transported by pipeline and injected deep underground into old gas and oil fields or porous rocks sealed by impermeable cap rock. This lets fossil fuels continue to be used while cutting the carbon dioxide released, but the technology is expensive and the long-term safety of storage has to be guaranteed.

bullets: A tax gives firms a financial reason to emit less because every tonne emitted costs money.
A licence or permit caps the total emissions allowed; firms that emit less than their permit may sell the spare to others (an emissions trading idea).
Advantage: it works through the market, so firms find the cheapest ways to cut emissions.
Disadvantage: firms may pass costs to consumers (higher prices for energy and goods) or **move production abroad** to countries without taxes, which just moves the emissions.
Political issue: voters may oppose higher bills, so governments may be unwilling to introduce them.
Fairness issue: poorer households spend a bigger share of income on energy, so they can be hit harder.
core.h: Reducing the footprint: carbon taxes and licences
core.p: Governments can use money as a tool. A **carbon tax** makes companies pay for each tonne of carbon dioxide they emit, and **carbon licences** (permits) give a limit to the amount of carbon dioxide an organisation may release. Both make polluting more expensive so that companies are encouraged to cut emissions or invest in cleaner technology. Their success depends on setting the right price or limit and on countries cooperating.

bullets: **Plant trees** (afforestation) and protect forests so more carbon dioxide is removed by photosynthesis.
**Reduce, reuse, recycle**: recycling metals and glass uses less energy than extracting and processing new materials, and keeping waste out of landfill reduces methane.
Capture methane from landfill sites and burn it to generate electricity: this converts methane to the less powerful greenhouse gas carbon dioxide and replaces fossil fuel.
Eat less beef and lamb and reduce food waste, cutting methane from livestock and landfill.
Buy local and seasonal goods to cut transport emissions, although transport is not always the largest part of a food's footprint.
Walk, cycle, use public transport or share lifts.
Improve rice farming methods (such as draining paddies periodically) to lower methane.
core.h: Other ways to lower a footprint
core.p: The specification highlights alternative energy, efficiency, capture and taxes, but exam answers may also use other sensible ideas. Individuals, businesses and governments can all reduce emissions, and a strong answer shows how the action reduces CO2 or methane specifically, not just that it is 'good for the environment'.

bullets: **Scientific**: technology such as CCS and large-scale energy storage is not yet fully developed; climate models carry uncertainty, so some people doubt how much action is needed; measuring a full footprint is difficult.
**Political**: governments need international agreement and cannot easily force other countries to act; leaders may avoid unpopular measures because of elections.
**Economic**: cleaner technology and infrastructure cost a great deal; businesses fear losing competitiveness; fossil fuels are often cheap.
**Social**: people dislike changing lifestyle (driving less, eating less meat, higher bills); lack of public awareness; jobs depend on fossil fuel industries.
**Ethical**: should rich countries that caused most historic emissions cut more than developing countries that want to grow? Is it fair to burden future generations?
Time lag: even if emissions stop, the carbon dioxide already released stays in the atmosphere for a long time.
core.p: If these actions were easy, carbon footprints would already be small. You need to be able to give reasons why progress is limited, and the specification groups them as **scientific, political, economic, social and ethical** issues. A good answer picks a reason and explains it in context rather than listing the five words.

bullets: Fossil fuels add 'new' carbon dioxide because the carbon was locked away for millions of years, so burning them increases atmospheric CO2.
Biofuels recycle carbon that was recently in the atmosphere, so the net addition is smaller.
Farming biofuel crops uses fertiliser (making it releases carbon dioxide; fertiliser in soil can release other greenhouse gases) and fuel for machinery.
Clearing forest to grow biofuel crops removes a carbon store, which can make the footprint worse.
Offsetting means paying for trees or renewable projects to balance your emissions; critics say it does not reduce your own emissions.
core.p: A process is called **carbon neutral** if the carbon dioxide it releases is balanced by the carbon dioxide removed from the air, giving no net addition. Biofuels are sometimes described this way because growing plants absorb carbon dioxide by photosynthesis that is released when the fuel is burned. In reality the full life cycle (fertiliser, machinery, transport, processing) emits greenhouse gases, so biofuels are often described as 'low carbon' rather than perfectly carbon neutral.

bullets: Always quote values **with units** from a table or graph when you compare options.
To find a percentage reduction use: (original - new) / original x 100.
For a total footprint, add emissions from every stage; for a journey, emissions = distance x emissions per km.
In an evaluate question use a structure: 'One advantage is... because... However... Overall...'.
Be careful with correlation: a product with a bigger footprint is not always 'worse' if it lasts much longer or does more.
Look for hidden stages: the data may exclude manufacture or disposal, which affects fairness of a comparison.
core.p: Carbon footprint questions often give you a table, bar chart or graph of emissions for different stages, products or choices. Read the units (kg or tonnes of CO2), compare the values with figures from the data, and then use ideas from the specification to explain the pattern. When a question asks you to evaluate, you must give both advantages and disadvantages and then reach a justified conclusion.

bullets: **Global climate change** (4.9.2): the greenhouse effect and the evidence for human influence explain why footprints matter.
**Fossil fuels and combustion** (4.7 and 4.9.3.2): burning hydrocarbons gives carbon dioxide and water; limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide and soot.
**Life cycle assessment** (4.10.1): the idea of assessing every stage of a product's life is the same idea used to compute a footprint.
**Using resources**: recycling metals and glass reduces the energy and emissions of extraction.
**Rates and energy**: catalysts let industry operate at lower temperatures, saving fuel.
**Photosynthesis and respiration** (Biology): the carbon cycle shows how carbon dioxide is removed and returned.
**Physics**: efficiency = useful energy out / total energy in; renewable energy resources.
core.p: Carbon footprints sit at the meeting point of several parts of the course, and examiners enjoy questions that connect them. Linking ideas also helps you remember the content because each action has a chemical or physical reason behind it.

exam: **Define** (1 mark): learn 'total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event'.
**State/Give** (1 mark): one precise point, e.g. 'wind power' or 'carbon capture and storage'; avoid vague answers like 'use less energy'.
**Describe** actions (2 marks): name the action and say what it does, e.g. 'use of wind turbines instead of burning fossil fuels, so less carbon dioxide is released'.
**Explain** (2 to 3 marks): use 'because' or 'so', linking action -> effect on CO2 or methane -> effect on footprint.
**Name the stages** of a life cycle: raw materials, manufacture, transport, use, disposal; give a gas or fuel burned at each stage for full marks.
**Evaluate/Discuss** (4 to 6 marks): give at least two advantages and two disadvantages with reasons, then a conclusion that makes a judgement using words like 'overall'.
**Why actions are limited**: use scientific, political, economic, social and ethical headings; give an example linked to the context.
**Calculations**: show working, include units (kg or tonnes of CO2), and give percentage change as change / original x 100.
**Graph questions**: quote values with units from the data, and describe the trend before explaining it.
Link with the **greenhouse effect** if asked about why it matters: short-wavelength in, long-wavelength infrared out and absorbed by greenhouse gases.
Avoid 'carbon' on its own when you mean carbon dioxide; examiners penalise confusion with the element or with carbon monoxide.

mistakes.r: It is the total carbon dioxide AND OTHER GREENHOUSE GASES over the FULL LIFE CYCLE of a product, service or event.
mistakes.w: The carbon footprint is the amount of carbon dioxide produced by a person.

mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming; the toxic gas is carbon monoxide.
mistakes.w: Carbon dioxide is a poisonous pollutant that damages lungs.

mistakes.r: They release no carbon dioxide during generation, but building, transporting and decommissioning them has a footprint.
mistakes.w: Wind turbines have no carbon footprint at all.

mistakes.r: Fossil fuels are still burned; the carbon dioxide is captured and stored so it does not enter the atmosphere.
mistakes.w: Carbon capture stops fossil fuels being burned.

mistakes.r: Give both sides: they encourage reduced emissions, but can raise costs, cause firms to relocate and affect poorer people more.
mistakes.w: Carbon taxes are bad because they make things expensive. (no reasoning)

mistakes.r: Recycling uses energy, but usually less than extracting and processing new raw materials, so it lowers the footprint.
Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas; each molecule traps much more heat, so cutting methane matters.
mistakes.w: Methane is not important because there is less of it than carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: Ozone depletion is a different issue; the carbon footprint is about greenhouse gases and global warming.
mistakes.w: The ozone layer problem is the same as the carbon footprint.

mistakes.r: Emissions occur at every life cycle stage: raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal.
mistakes.w: The only emissions are from using the product.

summary: You need to know that the carbon footprint is the total carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event, how it can be reduced (alternative energy, efficiency, carbon capture and storage, carbon taxes and licences), and why these actions are limited by scientific, political, economic, social and ethical issues. It matters because examiners ask you to evaluate real decisions about climate change.

terms.d: The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
A gas in the atmosphere (such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour) that absorbs long-wavelength infrared radiation and radiates some back to Earth, keeping it warmer.
All the stages in the life of a product: obtaining raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal.
A fuel formed over millions of years from the remains of living organisms, such as coal, crude oil and natural gas; burning it releases carbon dioxide.
Burning: a reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen, releasing energy.
The clearing of forests, which reduces the amount of carbon dioxide removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis.
An energy source that is used instead of fossil fuels, such as wind, solar, hydroelectric, nuclear or biofuel.
The proportion of energy supplied that is transferred usefully; improving it means less fuel is needed for the same job.
Removing carbon dioxide from waste gases and storing it, usually deep underground, so that it does not enter the atmosphere.
A charge made by government on organisations for each unit of carbon dioxide they release.
A permit that limits the amount of carbon dioxide an organisation is allowed to emit.
A fuel made from plant or animal material, such as bioethanol or biodiesel.
Having no net release of carbon dioxide because emissions are balanced by carbon dioxide removed from the atmosphere.
CH4, the main component of natural gas and a greenhouse gas released by livestock, rice paddy fields and landfill sites.
A long-term change in the Earth's climate, including temperature rise, linked to increased greenhouse gases.
Evaluation of scientific work by other scientists before it is published, to check it is valid.

worked.q: A commuter drives 12 km to work and 12 km home, 5 days a week for 46 weeks. The car emits 0.18 kg of carbon dioxide per km. Calculate the carbon dioxide emitted in a year by the commute. (3 marks)

worked.q: A company reduces its yearly footprint from 8.0 tonnes of carbon dioxide to 6.2 tonnes. Calculate the percentage reduction. (2 marks)

worked.ans: Model answer: CCS captures carbon dioxide from the flue gases of a power station, compresses it and stores it in rock underground, so much less carbon dioxide enters the atmosphere and the carbon footprint of the electricity falls. It lets existing fossil fuel stations continue to supply reliable electricity. However, the process needs a lot of extra energy, is expensive, requires suitable storage sites, and the gas could leak. Overall, CCS is useful as a short-term measure, but because it is costly and does not remove emissions from mining and transport, it should be used alongside renewable energy and improved energy efficiency.
worked.q: Evaluate the use of carbon capture and storage (CCS) to reduce the carbon footprint of electricity generation. (6 marks)
steps: Advantage: removes most carbon dioxide from the power station's waste gases so the amount reaching the atmosphere is greatly reduced.
Advantage: existing power stations can keep operating, so electricity supply stays reliable while the country builds other low-carbon supplies.
Disadvantage: the capture, compression and transport need energy, so extra fuel is burned.
Disadvantage: very expensive to build and run, which may raise electricity prices.
Disadvantage: storage sites are limited and carbon dioxide could leak back out, so long-term monitoring is needed.
Conclusion: CCS can help in the short term but is best combined with renewable energy and efficiency.
